summary: Describes IP fragmentation and explains why it makes Internet communication fragile. It proposes alternatives to fragmentation and gives recommendations to developers and network operators. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8900 explains why splitting an IP packet into fragments is risky in practice. A fragment carries only part of the original packet, so the devices along the path often cannot tell what it is or where it should go. The RFC lists the failures it has seen, the attacks it enables, and the alternatives: size the transport segments to the path, and probe the path for its real limit instead of relying on ICMP messages that may be lost.

questions: why do icmp packet too big messages get lost
subtitle: Why splitting IP packets into fragments breaks so often on the real Internet, and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: When a packet is bigger than a path can carry, IP can split it into fragments. Many devices on the path handle fragments badly, so fragmented traffic is dropped, misrouted, abused by attackers or corrupted.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues the ways fragmentation fails (routing, NAT, firewalls, load balancing, ID collisions, attacks, lost ICMP messages), then describes alternatives such as keeping transport segments small and probing the path MTU.
tldr.outcome: It does not deprecate fragmentation, but tells developers not to build new protocols that depend on it and tells operators to keep PMTUD working.

today: RFC 8900 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted or updated. It deliberately stops short of deprecating IP fragmentation and instead tells new protocols to avoid relying on it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Operational experience shows that IP fragmentation introduces fragility to Internet communication. This document describes IP fragmentation and explains the fragility it introduces. It also proposes alternatives to IP fragmentation and provides recommendations for developers and network operators.

While the document identifies issues associated with IP fragmentation, it does not recommend deprecation. Legacy protocols that depend on IP fragmentation would do well to be updated to remove that dependency. Some applications and environments still require IP fragmentation, and in those cases the protocol will continue to rely on it, but the designer should be aware that fragmented packets may result in black holes. A design should include appropriate safeguards.

Rather than deprecating IP fragmentation, the document recommends that upper-layer protocols address the problem of fragmentation at their layer, reducing their reliance on IP fragmentation to the greatest degree possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not say that IP fragmentation should be removed from the Internet. It says the same thing in a different way: new protocols should not depend on it, old ones should be fixed where that is possible, and where a protocol cannot avoid it, the design has to expect that fragments can be lost.

sections.title: Links, Paths, MTU and PMTU
sections.content:
An Internet path connects a source node to a destination node and may contain several links and routers, with the links connected in series. Internet paths are dynamic: if a link or a router fails, the path can change to use a different set of links and routers.

Each link is constrained by the number of octets it can carry in one IP packet, which is called the link Maximum Transmission Unit, or MTU. IPv4 requires every link to support an MTU of 68 octets or greater, and IPv6 requires every link to support an MTU of 1280 octets or greater. These are the IPv4 and IPv6 minimum link MTUs.

Each path is constrained by the number of octets it can carry in one IP packet, which is called the Path MTU, or PMTU. For any given path the PMTU equals the smallest of its link MTUs, and because paths change, the PMTU changes too.

Source nodes therefore estimate the PMTU. A source can produce extremely conservative estimates in which the estimate for each IPv4 path equals the IPv4 minimum link MTU and the estimate for each IPv6 path equals the IPv6 minimum link MTU. Those estimates are guaranteed to be no larger than the real PMTU, but they are likely to be much smaller, which can hurt the performance of the protocol above.

Path MTU Discovery, or PMTUD, keeps a less conservative estimate. The source starts with an estimate equal to the MTU of the first link on the path, which can be greater than the actual PMTU, and sends non-fragmentable packets. If a packet is larger than the actual PMTU, the downstream router cannot forward it, drops it, and sends the source an ICMP Packet Too Big message carrying the MTU of the link that could not carry it. The source then refines its estimate. Because the PMTU is dynamic, the estimate can be too large, so PMTUD occasionally resets the estimate to its initial value and repeats the procedure to detect increases.

PMTUD fails in some scenarios. It relies on the network delivering ICMP Packet Too Big messages to the source, and it is susceptible to attack because ICMP messages are easily forged and are not authenticated by the receiver. Such attacks can make the estimate unnecessarily conservative.
sections.plainLanguage: Every link has a size limit, and the path limit is the smallest of them. A sender does not know that limit, so it estimates it. The usual method, Path MTU Discovery, sends a packet that cannot be split and waits for the router that cannot forward it to report the limit back. That method fails when those reports are lost, and it can be pushed towards a too-small estimate by forged messages.

sections.title: How Fragmentation Works
sections.content:
When an upper-layer protocol submits data to the IP module and the resulting IP packet is longer than the PMTU, the packet is divided into fragments. Each fragment includes an IP header and a portion of the original packet.

In IPv4, a packet whose Don't Fragment bit is set to 1 may be fragmented by the source node but not by a downstream router, while a packet whose Don't Fragment bit is set to 0 may be fragmented by the source node or by a downstream router. When an IPv4 packet is fragmented, all the IP options appear in the first fragment, but only the options whose copy bit is set to 1 appear in later fragments.

In IPv6, a packet may be fragmented only at the source node. When an IPv6 packet is fragmented, all the extension headers appear in the first fragment, but only the per-fragment headers appear in later fragments. The per-fragment headers are the IPv6 header, the Hop-by-Hop Options header if present, the Destination Options header if present and if it precedes a Routing header, the Routing header if present, and the Fragment header.

In IPv4 the upper-layer header usually appears in the first fragment, because of the sizes of the headers involved. In IPv6 the upper-layer header must appear in the first fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting a packet means sending several smaller packets, each with its own IP header. In IPv4 any router along the path may do the splitting, unless the sender marked the packet as indivisible. In IPv6 only the sender may split, and the pieces carry only the headers that every piece needs, which is why the later pieces often no longer show which port or protocol the traffic belongs to.

sections.title: Where Fragments Break
sections.content:
The RFC lists several places where fragmentation causes trouble.

Virtual reassembly is a procedure in which a device conceptually reassembles a packet, forwards its fragments and discards the reassembled copy. It is required in Address plus Port NAT and in Carrier Grade NAT to translate fragment addresses correctly. It is computationally expensive and holds state for indeterminate periods of time, so it is prone to errors and attacks.

Policy-based routing breaks because the port information is only in the first fragment. A router looks up the next hop in its forwarding information base. With the example table in the RFC, the first fragment of a packet for TCP port 80 matches both the destination-based entry and the more specific policy-based entry, so it goes to the policy next hop. The second fragment carries no port information, so only the destination-based entry matches and the fragment goes to the other next hop. The two halves of one packet then travel different ways.

Network address translation has the same root cause. A NAT device maps the source port and address of a new outbound flow and translates the headers on the way out and the way back, and it must virtually reassemble fragmented packets to translate and forward each fragment.

Stateless firewalls whose rules include TCP and UDP ports see the port only in the first fragment. The firewall can accept all the later fragments, possibly admitting certain classes of attack, or block them all, possibly blocking legitimate traffic. Neither option is attractive.

Equal-cost multipath, link aggregation groups and stateless load balancers assign each packet or fragment to a link with a hash algorithm. When the fragment contains a transport-layer header the algorithm uses the source address, destination address, protocol or next header, and the two ports. When it does not, the algorithm uses only the source address, destination address and protocol. Non-fragmented packets of one flow can therefore go to one link while the fragments of the same flow are divided between that link and another, which causes suboptimal load distribution. RFC 6438 offers a partial solution for IPv6 devices only, by requiring the hash to include at least the destination address, source address and flow label, which sends all fragments of a packet to the same link.

IPv4 reassembly errors at high data rates are the last problem. The 16-bit IPv4 identification field is not large enough at high data rates to prevent duplicate IDs, so fragments are assembled incorrectly, and the TCP and UDP checksums are not sufficient to stop the corrupted datagrams from reaching the upper layer. These issues are less frequent in IPv6, whose identification field is 32 bits long.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the trouble comes from the same fact: only the first fragment carries the information that identifies the traffic. A router that forwards by port, a NAT device that rewrites addresses and ports, a firewall that filters by port, and a load balancer that hashes the flow all have to make a decision on a fragment that no longer says what it is. The result is packets that go to the wrong place, or get dropped, or get spread over links unevenly.

sections.title: Attacks That Exploit Fragments
sections.content:
Security researchers have documented several attacks that exploit IP fragmentation. The RFC lists overlapping fragment attacks, resource exhaustion attacks, attacks based on predictable fragment identification values, and evasion of network intrusion detection systems.

In the overlapping fragment attack, an attacker constructs a series of packet fragments. The first fragment contains an IP header, a transport-layer header and some transport-layer payload, so it complies with the local security policy and is allowed through a stateless firewall. A second fragment with a nonzero offset overlaps with the first and also passes the firewall. When the packet is reassembled, the transport-layer header from the first fragment is overwritten by data from the second, and the reassembled packet no longer complies with the local security policy. Had it passed through the firewall in one piece, the firewall would have rejected it.

A stateless firewall cannot protect against the overlapping fragment attack, but destination nodes can, by implementing the reassembly procedures of RFC 1858, RFC 3128 and RFC 8200, which detect the overlap and discard the packet.

The fragment reassembly algorithm is a stateful procedure in an otherwise stateless protocol, so it can be exploited by resource exhaustion attacks. An attacker constructs a series of fragmented packets with one fragment missing from each, so the reassembly never completes. This causes resource exhaustion on the destination node, possibly denying reassembly service to other flows. The attack can be mitigated by flushing the fragment reassembly buffers when necessary, at the price of possibly dropping legitimate fragments.

Each fragment also carries an Identification field that the destination uses to reassemble. Some implementations set that field to a predictable value, which makes it easy to forge fragments that cause the reassembly procedure for legitimate packets to fail. Finally, the ambiguity of what the reassembled packet will be allows an attacker to evade network intrusion detection systems, many of which try to reduce that evasion by computing all possible reassembly outcomes at the cost of more processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Fragments give an attacker two useful tricks. One is to send a fragment that overlaps another one, so that the packet the firewall approved is not the packet the destination ends up with. The other is to send fragments that never complete, which ties up the memory the destination keeps for reassembly. The firewall cannot stop either, so the protection has to be at the destination, and the session itself has to be protected.

sections.title: Black Holes from Lost ICMP Messages
sections.content:
An upper-layer protocol that relies on PMTUD also relies on the network to deliver ICMP Packet Too Big messages, and that delivery is not reliable. It is subject to both transient and persistent loss.

Transient loss causes transient PMTU black holes: when the conditions causing the loss abate, the network regains the ability to deliver the messages and connectivity is restored. The causes are network congestion, packet corruption, transient routing loops and ICMP rate limiting. Rate limiting can be severe, because RFC 4443 recommends strict rate limiting of ICMPv6 traffic.

Persistent loss causes persistent black holes, and the RFC names three causes. The first is an incorrect implementation of a security policy: a zone-based policy that allows traffic from the outside zone only if it belongs to an existing flow should check the payload of the ICMP message to see whether the original packet belonged to an existing flow, but an incorrect implementation discards the message because its source address is not associated with an existing flow. The RFC notes that this policy has been implemented incorrectly on many consumer CPE routers.

The second is anycast. A DNS client sends a request to an anycast address, which the network routes to the nearest instance. The response does not exceed that server's PMTU estimate but does exceed the actual PMTU, so a downstream router drops it and sends the ICMP message to the anycast address. The message is then routed to the anycast instance closest to that router, which may be a different server from the one that sent the response, so the server that needs the information never learns the smaller limit.

The third is unidirectional routing: if the intermediate nodes have a route to the destination but not back to the source, an intermediate node that hits an MTU problem cannot send the message to the source at all.

Fragments are also lost for other reasons. The study in RFC 7872 found that at least 28% of the sampled paths did not convey packets containing the IPv6 Fragment extension header, with the fragments usually dropped in the destination autonomous system and sometimes in transit ones. Another study reported that 37% of sampled endpoints used IPv6-capable DNS resolvers that could not receive a fragmented IPv6 response. The RFC lists possible causes: hardware inability to process fragmented packets, failure to change vendor defaults, unintentional misconfiguration, and intentional configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Path MTU Discovery only works if the too-big messages get back to the sender, and they often do not. Congestion, rate limiting and broken firewall rules lose them for a while, and anycast or one-way routing loses them for good. The result is a connection that silently stops working, because both ends believe the path can carry their packets.

sections.title: Alternatives to IP Fragmentation
sections.content:
Transport-layer solutions. TCP can be operated so that IP fragmentation is never needed. Applications give TCP a stream, TCP divides it into segments no larger than the TCP Maximum Segment Size, and if the MSS is small enough the IP module never produces a packet longer than the actual PMTU. TCP offers three mechanisms for managing the MSS: manual configuration, PMTUD, and PLPMTUD. Manual configuration always works but stops TCP from using larger link MTUs. PMTUD needs the network to deliver ICMP messages, so it can only be used where that risk is acceptable. PLPMTUD does not depend on ICMP messages: it sends probe messages as TCP segments and checks that they are acknowledged, and it separates probing from congestion control so that a lost probe does not shrink the congestion window.

The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol and the Stream Control Transmission Protocol can also be operated without IP fragmentation, and both offer manual configuration, PMTUD and PLPMTUD for managing their maximum segment size. UDP has no fragmentation mechanism of its own and relies on IP fragmentation, though a UDP fragmentation mechanism has been proposed.

Application-layer solutions. The UDP usage guidelines of RFC 8085 say that an application should not send UDP datagrams that would result in IP packets larger than the MTU on the path, and should either use the path MTU information from the IP layer or implement PMTU discovery itself. An application that does not do discovery should still avoid oversized datagrams and fall back to sending messages shorter than the default effective MTU for sending. For IPv4 that value is the smaller of 576 bytes and the first-hop MTU, and for IPv6 it is 1280 bytes. The same advice applies to any application running directly over IP.

Applications that still rely on IPv6 fragmentation are DNS, OSPFv2, OSPFv3 and packet-in-packet encapsulations. Some of that reliance is essential and cannot be broken without changing the protocol, while some is incidental and most implementations already avoid it. DNS relies on UDP for efficiency, which means large responses are fragmented; the mitigation is to use smaller EDNS0 buffer sizes or to limit the response size, so that large responses are truncated and the client re-queries over TCP. Most OSPF implementations restrict their maximum message size so that no fragmentation is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways out. A transport protocol can keep its own segments small enough that IP never has to split anything, and it can find the real path limit by probing rather than by waiting for ICMP messages. An application using UDP can do the same thing itself, or fall back to sending small messages. Some protocols, such as DNS and OSPF, cannot avoid the issue entirely, so their operators have to make sure the fragments are not dropped.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
For application and protocol developers: developers should not develop new protocols or applications that rely on IP fragmentation, and a new protocol or application deployed in an environment that does not fully support fragmentation should operate correctly, either by default or in a specified alternative configuration. Legacy protocols that depend on fragmentation should be updated to break the dependency, but where there is no viable alternative, such as in IPsec tunnel mode or IP-in-IP encapsulation, the protocol will continue to rely on fragmentation and should only be used in environments where fragmentation is known to be supported. Protocols can avoid fragmentation by using a sufficiently small MTU, disabling IP fragmentation, and making sure the transport protocol adapts its segment size to the MTU, or by deploying a sufficiently reliable PMTU discovery mechanism such as PLPMTUD. UDP applications should follow the guidance in Section 3.2 of RFC 8085.

For system developers: software libraries should include provision for PLPMTUD for each supported transport protocol.

For middlebox developers: middleboxes should process IP fragments in a manner consistent with RFC 791 and RFC 8200. Price and performance often lead operators to deploy stateless middleboxes, which may process fragments suboptimally, in a way that is not compliant with those specifications, or discard fragments completely. Such behaviour is not recommended, and any non-standard behaviour with respect to fragmentation must be clearly documented.

For ECMP, LAG and load-balancer developers and operators: in their default configuration, when the IPv6 flow label is not zero, devices that implement ECMP, link aggregation or other load-distribution technologies should accept only the IP source address, the IP destination address and the flow label as input to their hash algorithm, and operators should deploy these devices in that default configuration. The RFC notes that these recommendations are similar to those of RFC 6438 and RFC 7098, but specify a default configuration.

For network operators: operators must ensure proper PMTUD operation in their network, including making sure the network generates Packet Too Big messages when dropping packets that are too large for the outgoing interface, although implementations may rate limit the generation of ICMP messages. Operators must not filter ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages unless they are known to be forged or otherwise illegitimate, because filtering them causes PMTUD to fail and many upper-layer protocols rely on it. Operators must not deploy IPv6 links whose MTU is less than 1280 octets, and should not filter IP fragments known to have come from or to be destined for a domain name server, because domain name services are critical to the operation of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendations are addressed to five groups. Protocol designers should not rely on fragmentation and should size their own packets instead. Library writers should build in packetization layer discovery. Middlebox writers should handle fragments correctly or say clearly that they do not. Load-balancer makers and operators should hash on the address pair and the flow label so that fragments of one packet stay together. Network operators must keep the too-big messages flowing and must not drop fragments to and from name servers.

items.title: Protocol developers
items.text: Do not rely on IP fragmentation, and adapt the transport segment size to the path instead.

items.title: System developers
items.text: Provide packetization layer PMTU discovery in the libraries for each transport protocol.

items.title: Middlebox developers
items.text: Process fragments as RFC 791 and RFC 8200 require, or document any other behaviour.

items.title: Load-balancer makers and operators
items.text: Hash on the address pair and the IPv6 flow label, and deploy that default configuration.

items.title: Network operators
items.text: Keep Packet Too Big messages flowing, keep IPv6 link MTUs at 1280 or more, and not drop fragments to or from name servers.
